parts.title: The tuatara-past and future
parts.article:
The tuatara – past and future
 
(A) The New Zealand species of lizard, the tuatara, is firmly embedded in the national psyche: an icon for today which dates from the age of dinosaurs; an ancient reptile commemorated on the back of the five-cent coin. New Zealanders feel an affinity with the tuatara, and accept that active conservation management is required to ensure it will be among the legacies left to future generations. When European explorers reached New Zealand in 1769 they found two large islands, which together they called the mainland, and many tiny offshore islands around the coast. The naturalists who came with the explorers disregarded the tuatara, though it is improbable none were seen. Only several decades later did a tuatara specimen reach the British Museum, where it was eventually classified as just another type of lizard.
 
(B) One of the first scientists who realised that aspects of tuatara anatomy were odd—unchanged for tens of thousands of years—was Albert Gunther in 1876. Gunther believed the tuatara was one of the most valuable objects in zoological anatomical collections, and also noted, in passing, the reptile was likely to become extinct. From today's perspective, it is striking that Gunther expressed no concern about the probable demise of the tuatara. He and his contemporaries were products of their age, strongly influenced by Charles Darwin's theory, which had only recently been published. Their views were something like this: 'Extinction is a natural process. It is sad that species disappear, but that is part of nature.'
 
(C) There is a second important aspect of Gunther's work. He recorded, correctly, that some of the mammals introduced by Europeans were predators of the tuatara—particularly rats. But what he did not realise was that New Zealand has two species of rat, both introduced, both with an appetite for tuatara: the ship's rat came with European explorers and settlers; but the kiore rat had already been in the country for hundreds of years, brought by Polynesians from the Pacific Islands. Gunther failed to recognise the distinction, believing all rats to be a relatively recent introduction. Little further research was conducted until Ian Crook of the NZ Wildlife Service published his findings in 1973, which can be summarised as follows. Tuatara thrive on offshore islands with no rats. Tuatara never survived on islands with ship's rats. On a few islands, small and declining populations of tuatara occur with the kiore. This should not be seen, however, as evidence that tuatara and kiore can coexist. Rather, Crook proposed, kiore probably only arrived recently on such islands, and thus the small populations represent extinctions in progress.
 
(D) Throughout the 1990s, Richard Holdaway and his colleagues at Victoria University in Wellington documented the surprising discovery that kiore probably arrived about 1,800 years ago, although the human population of New Zealand is thought to be no older than 800 years. How is this possible? Presumably, Holdaway argued, the kiore were brought by Polynesian explorers who visited the country but did not settle. Thereafter, the rats were agents of ecological warfare, exterminating perhaps 1,000–3,000 species. Thus, tuatara and many other species were already rare or extinct when permanent human inhabitants—the Maori—arrived around 1300. This hypothesis is still being debated, but the evidence continues to accumulate in its favour.
 
(E) Conservation practice has changed dramatically since Crook's findings were published in 1973. Eradication of rats from any given environment was believed to be virtually impossible until about 1980, but since then has become routine. Enormous conservation benefits are accruing as newly rat-free offshore islands are providing sanctuaries for the country's rarest species. In 1995, for example, Nicola Nelson of the Department of Conservation established 68 tuatara on Titi Island. Since then, four more populations of tuatara have been established elsewhere under similar conditions. Today, numbers of tuatara are still a fraction of what they once were, but for the first time in 1,800 years the decline has been reversed.
 
(F) While the recovery of rare species is itself a good thing, the truly significant outcome of this research is that it liberates the imagination. If we can remove predatory introduced mammals from islands, why not from the mainland too? Perhaps the questions we ask should demonstrate even more visionary ambition. Can non-mammalian pests also be removed from the mainland? Our rivers, for example, are full of surrogate rats, in the form of introduced species of fish called trout. Some day more people will understand that trout have replaced a whole native fauna in our waterways, just as rats replaced tuatara on the mainland. Will such knowledge lead to the creation of mainland 'aquatic islands' where we can once again establish those species of indigenous fish that used to live in our rivers? Similarly, can bellbirds and tuis replace birds like starlings and mynahs? The answers to such questions are uncertain, and opposing sides will doubtless be fiercely debated. But the role of scientific knowledge in illuminating the past will be crucial. Just as we no longer tolerate extinction, in the future we may no longer accept a mainland devoid of the biological wonders of our past such as tuatara. Conservation is thus not primarily about the past but about imagining and then creating the future we wish for our children and ourselves. For 80 million years until humans arrived, tuatara occurred throughout New Zealand—might they do so again?
parts.questions:
Questions 27–31
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 27-31 on your answer sheet.

Q27 What are we told about the Europeans who arrived in 1769?

  • A They thought there was only one large island.
  • B They had not come to study natural history.
  • C They had no interest in the tuatara.
  • D They sent a tuatara to the British Museum.

Q28 What does the writer say about Albert Gunther in the second paragraph?

  • A He believed the tuatara could fetch a high price.
  • B He was typical of his generation of scientists.
  • C He disagreed with Charles Darwin's theory.
  • D He wanted to stop the tuatara becoming extinct.

Q29 What did Albert Gunther think about the rats in New Zealand?

  • A They did not eat the tuatara.
  • B There was one species of rat.
  • C There had always been rats in New Zealand.
  • D They were killed by Polynesians.

Q30 What did Ian Crook conclude from his research?

  • A Tuatara are safe on small islands.
  • B Ship's rats kill more tuatara than kiore.
  • C Kiore cannot swim to offshore islands.
  • D Rats and tuatara cannot live together.

Q31 What were the findings of Richard Holdaway's research?

  • A Maori settled more recently than previously thought.
  • B The first Polynesian explorers formed permanent settlements.
  • C Ship's rats are the oldest rat species in the country.
  • D Rats caused extinctions before any humans settled.
Questions 32–35
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 32-35 on your answer sheet, write:

Q32 The available research supports Holdaway's theory but it has not been proved.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q33 Nowadays, it is possible to totally destroy a population of rats on a small island.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q34 Crook was the first person to recognise the potential of offshore islands as sanctuaries.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q35 Tuatara numbers are continuing to fall.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 36–40
Complete the summary using the list of words, A-H, below.
Write the correct letter, A-H, in boxes 36-40 on your answer sheet.
What conclusions can we draw?
The most important result of the tuatara research is that it frees our . For example, there are many similarities between rats and . Should we now go further and consider reintroducing to our mainland rivers? Perhaps our children will come to believe in the of species, in the same way that our generation refuses to accept .
  • A natural evolution
  • B creative thought
  • C indigenous plants
  • D trout
  • E pollution
  • F restoration
  • G native fish
  • H extinction

reference:
Q27

干扰 A错，原文说“found two large islands”；B错，随行有“naturalists”就是为了研究；D错，标本是几十年后（Only several decades later）才送到博物馆的。

句子 (Paragraph A) “The naturalists who came with the explorers disregarded the tuatara...”

解析 题目问关于1769年到达的欧洲人我们得知了什么。A段提到随探险家来的博物学家“disregarded the tuatara（忽视了大蜥蜴）”，即对它没兴趣，对应选项 C。

Q28

解析 题目问第三段作者对Albert Gunther说了什么。B段指出Gunther和他的同代人是“products of their age（时代的产物）”，深受达尔文理论影响，即他是那一代科学家的典型代表，对应选项 B。

干扰 “Products of their age” 是 “typical of his generation” 的同义替换。他并未想阻止灭绝（D），也没反对达尔文（C）。

句子 (Paragraph B) “He and his contemporaries were products of their age... strongly influenced by Charles Darwin's theory...”

Q29

解析 题目问Albert Gunther对新西兰老鼠的看法。C段提到Gunther“failed to recognise the distinction（未能识别出区别）”，认为所有老鼠都是相对近期引入的，即认为只有一种，对应选项 B。

干扰 “One species of rat” 对应 “failed to recognise the distinction / believing all rats to be...”。

句子 (Paragraph C) “Gunther failed to recognise the distinction... believing all rats to be a relatively recent introduction.”

Q30

干扰 “Cannot live together” 对应原文的 “Should not be seen... as evidence that... can coexist”。

解析 题目问Ian Crook从研究中得出了什么结论。C段末尾提到Crook认为小规模并存代表正在进行的灭绝（extinctions in progress），不应视为共存证据，即老鼠和大蜥蜴不能共存，对应选项 D。

句子 (Paragraph C) “This should not be seen, however, as evidence that tuatara and kiore can coexist.”

Q31

解析 题目问Richard Holdaway的研究发现是什么。D段提到Holdaway认为在人类（毛利人）定居之前，老鼠已经导致了大量物种灭绝（exterminating... before the Maori arrived），对应选项 D。

干扰 “Before any humans settled” 对应 “before the Maori arrived / permanent human inhabitants”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “...the rats were agents of ecological warfare, exterminating... before the Maori arrived...”

Q32

解析 题目说现有研究支持Holdaway的理论但尚未证实。D段末尾说这个假设（hypothesis）仍在争论中，但“evidence continues to accumulate in its favour（证据继续对其有利地积累）”，即有支持但未定论，选 YES。

干扰 “Supports... but not proved” 对应 “evidence accumulates in its favour” 和 “still being debated”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “This hypothesis is still being debated, but the evidence continues to accumulate in its favour.”

Q33

句子 (Paragraph E) “Eradication of rats... has become routine.”

解析 题目说现在完全消灭小岛上的老鼠是可能的。E段提到彻底消灭老鼠（Eradication）自1980年左右以来已成为“routine（常规操作）”，即完全可能，选 YES。

干扰 “Possible to totally destroy” 对应 “Eradication... has become routine”。

Q34

解析 题目说Crook是第一个认识到离岸岛屿作为避难所潜力的人。文中只说Crook发表了发现，并未提及他是否是“first person to recognise the potential（第一个认识到潜力的人）”，信息缺失，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 不要看到名字就默认他是第一人，雅思必须要有“first”或等价表达。

Q35

解析 题目说大蜥蜴数量持续下降。E段末尾明确说，虽然数量仍少，但在1800年来首次“the decline has been reversed（下降已被扭转）”，即不再下降，选 NO。

干扰 “Reversed” 直接反驳了 “continuing to fall”。

句子 (Paragraph E) “...but for the first time in 1,800 years the decline has been reversed.”

Q36

解析 题目说研究最重要的结果是解放了我们的____。原文F段开头说这“liberates the imagination（解放了想象力）”，对应选项 B（创造性思维）。

干扰 “Imagination” ≈ “Creative thought”。

句子 (Paragraph F) “...it liberates the imagination.”

Q37

句子 (Paragraph F) “...surrogate rats, in the form of introduced species of fish called trout.”

解析 题目说老鼠和____之间有许多相似之处。原文F段把被引入的一种叫“trout（鳟鱼）”的鱼称为“surrogate rats（代理老鼠）”，即两者相似，填 D (trout)。

干扰 “Surrogate rats” 暗示了相似性。

Q38

解析 题目说我们是否应该考虑将____重新引入大陆河流。原文F段问是否能再次建立那些曾生活在我们河流中的“species of indigenous fish（本土鱼类）”，对应选项 G (native fish)。

干扰 “Indigenous” = “Native”。

句子 (Paragraph F) “...establish those species of indigenous fish that used to live in our rivers...”

Q39

解析 题目说也许孩子会相信物种的____。原文F段说保护不仅仅关于过去，而是关于“imagining and then creating the future（想象并创造未来）”，虽然没有直接词，但结合上文“reversed decline”和“reintroduce”，这是一种复苏/恢复的愿景，对应选项 F (restoration)。

干扰 全段都在讲恢复生态（remove pests, reintroduce natives），这是 restoration 的核心。

句子 (Paragraph F) 整体语境支持复苏/恢复。

Q40

解析 题目说就像我们这一代拒绝接受____一样。原文F段倒数第二句说“Just as we no longer tolerate extinction（就像我们不再容忍灭绝）”，填 H (extinction)。

干扰 “Refuses to accept” 对应 “no longer tolerate”。

句子 (Paragraph F) “Just as we no longer tolerate extinction...”
